messages.subject: Problems with expansions
messages.body_plain:
Hey everyone,

I'm new to using Distance. I'm trying to analyze trapping web data in ord=
er to get density estimates on small mammals to finish up my thesis. I'm =
using point counts , single objects, and meter/hectare for my distances. =
I've been getting reasonable density estimates, but I've been having issu=
es with the expansions. For example, when I analyze a data set using norm=
al, half-normal, etc., I get different density, confidence intervals, and=
 CV's. However, when I expand within those sets using the expansions cosi=
ne, simple polynomial, and hermite...I get the exact same numbers across =
the board. I know I should be getting different values and then be compar=
ing the AIC to determine which fits my data set best, but I can't figure =
out what I'm doing wrong. I've spent quite a while going through the arch=
ives so I don't think this has been an issue before. If it has, sorry for=
 the repeat, but I could really use some advice. Extremely stuck. Thanks!=

--

messages.subject: Re: Problems with expansions
messages.body_plain:
Hi Stephanie, (list)

I suspect that Distance is not choosing any adjustment terms.  The default in
Distance is to use a forward selection scheme, where it first fits the specified
key function, and then the key function plus one adjustment, and if AIC is
lower, it then tries key function plus two adjustment, etc.  It stops when AIC
does not get lower with the more complex model. In many cases, the key function
alone has a lower AIC than the key function + 1 adjustment model, so it just
stops with the key.  If you try another adjustment term and that also stops with
just the key, then you have exactly the same answer.

You can see how many adjustments were fit by browsing through the Results tab of
the Analysis details for each model.  Or, as a shortcut, look at the number of
parameters for each model in the Analysis Browser.  If, for example, for a half
normal+cosine model, the number of parameters is 1, then it means no adjustments
were used.

As an aside, it's become more fashionable recently to analyze trapping web data
using Spatially Explicit Capture Recapture methods (assuming you kept the
capture histories and have individually marked animals).  You'll find lots of
literature on this, and also Windows software (Density) and R packages (secr and
admbsecr, among others).

Cheers - Len

--

messages.subject: Re: Size-bias regression in R
messages.body_plain:
I don't have much familiarity with those 2 R packages but I have put
together some custom code  for size biased detection with "unmarked".
 Presumably this code could be modified for the other packages.

*# Get the detection probabilities by distance.*

*# **The DISTGROUP dataframe contains 2 columns: distance to*

*# detection (Dist) and group size (Size).*

*gx_hn=gxhn(DISTGROUP$Dist,exp(coef(hn,type="det")))*

*# Regress ln(group size) against detection probability.*

*size.bias_hn=lm(log(DISTGROUP$Size)~gx_hn)*

*summary(size.bias_hn)*

*# If significant at alpha=0.15, use adjusted mean group size.*

*adj.group.size_hn=exp(sum(size.bias_hn$coefficients)+*

*  ((1+(1/n)+((1-mean(DISTGROUP$Size))^2)/sum((gx_hn-*

*  mean(DISTGROUP$Size))^2))*mean(size.bias_hn$residuals^2))/2)*
Good Luck,

Matt

messages.subject: Re: Size-bias regression in R
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris, list,

I don't think there is anything built in to mrds or Distance that allows this
exactly (the authors of those packages will contradict me if I'm wrong), but a
good (perhaps even better) alternative would be to include cluster size as a
possible covariate in the detection function model.

One could write code to implement the old-style size bias regression models --
would also need code to propagate variance appropriately.  Let me know if you
want this and we can likely come up with something.

Cheers - Len

--

messages.subject: Re: Size-bias regression in R
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris & list,

Len is correct, including size as a covariate is the way we usually deal
with group size in mrds/Distance and the "old" size bias regression is
not included in the packages. It is sometimes necessary to "standardise"
the size covariate first (by dividing through by the standard deviation
of the size values) to avoid numerical issues.

Hope this helps,
--dave
